The must-sees

  • Augustusplatz

    Square

    The square was a major gathering point of the peaceful demonstrations of autumn 1989. Its buildings span from GDR modernism to the new university hall.

    Look for: The pointed glass gable of the university’s Paulinum recalls the church that once stood on that spot.

  • Gewandhaus

    Culture · 1981

    The orchestra goes back to 1743 and takes its name from the cloth merchants’ hall where it first played. Felix Mendelssohn was one of its conductors; the present hall opened in 1981.

    Look for: The ceiling painting seen through the glass is Sighard Gille’s Song of Life.

  • Leipzig Central Station

    Station · 1915

    Completed in 1915, it is one of the largest terminal stations in Europe by area. Its two great halls were once run by the Prussian and Saxon railways.

    Look for: Along one of the platforms, a museum track keeps historic locomotives on display.

  • Monument to the Battle of the Nations

    Landmark · 1913

    It was unveiled in 1913, a hundred years after the battle in which allied armies defeated Napoleon near Leipzig. A platform at the top looks out over the whole city.

    Look for: Down in the crypt, giant stone warriors with bowed heads stand guard over the fallen.

  • Mädler Passage

    Shopping

    The arcade was built in the 1910s on the site of an old trade hall. Goethe used Auerbachs Keller as a scene in his Faust, and bronze figures from the play stand at its stairs.

    Look for: In the rotunda, a glockenspiel with bells of Meissen porcelain chimes over the shoppers.

  • Old Town Hall

    Building

    It was built in the 1550s under Hieronymus Lotter, reportedly in less than a year. It now houses the museum of city history.

    Look for: Behind the town hall, on the Naschmarkt, a statue of the young Goethe recalls his student years in Leipzig.

  • St. Nicholas Church

    Church

    Monday peace prayers held here in the 1980s grew into the Monday demonstrations of 1989. On 9 October that year about 70,000 people marched peacefully around the ring road.

    Look for: In the churchyard outside stands a copy of one of the palm-topped columns, set up as a memorial to the protests of 1989.

  • St. Thomas Church

    Church

    Johann Sebastian Bach was cantor here from 1723 until his death in 1750, and his grave is in front of the altar. The St. Thomas Boys Choir still sings here every week.

    Look for: On the Bach statue outside, the left coat pocket is turned inside out, said to show how little money he had.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Leipzig and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Leipzig passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
